title: Neural Networks in Trading: Training Deep Spiking Models (Conclusion)
text:
Introduction
The financial market, like any complex nonlinear system, operates according to its own laws. It breathes, fluctuates, accumulates energy, and releases it in the form of sharp price movements. And the more closely we study its dynamics, the clearer it becomes that classical analytical methods can no longer always keep pace with the volatility of modern trading scenarios. A new generation of algorithms is taking their place — more sensitive, adaptive, and capable of seeing the market’s internal impulse beneath the surface of the chart.
In previous works, we have progressed from the basic principles of spiking computation to the implementation of key architectural solutions that pave the way for the practical use of such models in the
MQL5
environment. Today, we are approaching the final stage of this journey — the implementation of the approaches proposed by the authors of the
SEW ResNet
(
Spiking Elementary Weights Residual Network
) framework, as applied to the analysis and forecasting of financial time series.
SEW ResNet
owes its creation to the desire to combine the computational efficiency of spiking models with the robustness and depth of classic
ResNet
architectures. At the heart of this approach is the concept of
energy-balanced learning
, in which information is transmitted through a series of discrete pulses. Every spike carries weight-related meaning; every delay reflects the system's response to the signal. As a result, the model is not only more computationally efficient but also captures cause-and-effect relationships between events over time more accurately — which is particularly important for analyzing price impulses and bursts of market activity.
In the context of financial markets, this opens up new opportunities. After all, the market signal is spiking by nature. It is uneven, containing periods of silence and bursts of activity, where a single moment separates chaos from regularity. Under such conditions, classical neural networks often
get stuck on noise
or lose sensitivity during prolonged fluctuations.
SEW ResNet
, on the other hand, is designed to maintain responsiveness — it reacts only to truly significant changes in the data stream, naturally filtering out everything unnecessary.
In the previous stages, we built the foundation for the future architecture step by step. Each module we implemented became a building block in the framework's foundation, where technical rigor was combined with the intuitive logic of market processes.
The module for
spiking activation with adaptive thresholds
became the first key element of this system. Its function is to control the neuron's response to the incoming stream of signals by distinguishing important fluctuations from natural noise. In classical
spiking
models, activation is fixed and often responds identically to any change. We, on the other hand, took the approach of a biological prototype: the adaptive threshold changes depending on the intensity of the input pulses and the frequency of the spikes. As a result, the network learns to respond only when it is truly necessary, avoiding overfitting to random price fluctuations.
This has direct practical implications for the market. This mechanism allows the algorithm to operate reliably under conditions of high volatility, where traditional models often lose accuracy. When the chart is chaotic, the adaptive threshold acts as a built-in filter for market noise, helping the system maintain clarity and respond only to key trend changes.
The next step was the implementation of
a gating mechanism
responsible for regulating the neuron's sensitivity to the novelty of the incoming signal. Essentially,
the gate
determines how strongly the current signal should affect the buildup of membrane potential. In other words, it regulates the extent to which a new impulse contributes to the formation of the neuron's internal state. This gives the system dynamic flexibility. It is capable of responding differently to recurring and new patterns, gradually developing its own sense
of habituation to similar events
.
In financial market terms, this resembles the behavior of an experienced trader who does not react to every price movement but pays attention only to truly new signals that disrupt the established balance.
The gating mechanism
acts as a regulator of the model’s attentiveness — it determines when to amplify the response and when, conversely, to reduce it, thereby maintaining stable perception. This type of sensitivity control allows false signals to be filtered out without losing the ability to learn from actual changes in market dynamics.
The implementation of the approaches proposed by the authors of the
SEW ResNet
framework in our work is based on the
ResNeXt
architecture, modified to accommodate spiking dynamics and adaptive sensitivity. At the heart of this approach is the concept of multi-channel perception, in which each parallel branch of the model processes data from its own perspective, and the results are then carefully combined into a single vector of market perception. This approach allows the model not only to register a price movement but also to distinguish its nature, intensity, and direction — things that traders typically determine
by intuition
.
The key component of the model is the
Spike ResNeXt Bottleneck
module, which acts as a kind of
semantic filter
. It compresses the incoming stream of signals, passes it through a narrow channel, and then expands it back out — but now in a cleaned, structured form. Here, the concept of the classic
Bottleneck
takes on
a spiking dimension
. Each element of the block is capable of
deciding
when to respond and when to remain silent.
The
Bottleneck
implementation uses a dynamic array of
cBottleneck
components that form the block's computational path. Layers are created programmatically, based on user-defined parameters. The data stream undergoes a series of sequential transformations: convolution operations, normalization, spiking activation, and grouped convolutions. The entire chain is designed to provide a balanced combination of accuracy and response speed.
Equally important is the
Spike ResNeXt Residual
module, which is responsible for passing on accumulated experience. Its structure ensures correct dimensional alignment between the main path and the shortcut path, allowing information about previous states to be preserved without distortion. In a financial context, this is analogous to a trader's memory — the ability to recall what happened before the current impulse and adjust the response with history in mind.
The
Residual
block is implemented based on the same dynamic principle: if the input and output dimensions do not match, intermediate convolutional and normalization layers are added. This approach makes the architecture robust to changes in model parameters, allowing the network depth to be scaled freely without disrupting the internal logic of the signals.
A particular advantage of this approach is
energy efficiency
. The implemented zero-input check eliminates unnecessary computations when the market is silent. During periods of low volatility, many neurons simply do not fire, which reduces the load on the system and speeds up computations without sacrificing accuracy. This principle aligns with the natural economy of attention: the model focuses only on those areas of the market where something important is actually happening.
The combination of the multi-channel
ResNeXt
architecture and adaptive
SEW
spiking logic creates a unique hybrid in which mathematical precision meets market intuition. Each branch of the model is trained to form its own perspective on the data, and residual connections ensure that these perspectives are merged into a single solution. As a result, the model demonstrates robustness to noise and the ability to identify subtle patterns — the very faint signals that herald the emergence of a trend.
The practical value of this approach is clear: the model does not simply analyze the past, but
learns to recognize
moments when the market state changes. This provides an advantage in developing forecasting strategies, filtering out false signals, and automatically managing trading decisions.
The author’s visualization of the framework is shown below.
Key Principles of Implementation
After the individual modules had been implemented one by one, a natural question arose: how could we combine these elements into a single, cohesive architecture, where each part complements the others and the entire system functions as a unified whole?
However, we should not rush things here. The architecture should not merely connect blocks, but rather ensure
harmonious interaction between processing levels
, where low-level features seamlessly transition into more abstract market structures. Therefore, it makes sense to first examine the very foundation — the framework upon which our
spiking intelligence
will be built. As mentioned earlier, this framework was
ResNeXt
, known for its modular flexibility and high performance.
We took
ResNeXt
as the foundation, but gave it a spiking signal nature. In its classic form,
ResNeXt
analyzes data streams using parallel processing branches, each of which extracts a distinct aspect of the input data. In our implementation, these branches have been converted into spiking channels capable of independently adjusting their sensitivity and response frequency to market changes.
The
Spike Bottleneck
module already implements a basic sequence processing loop: the signal is compressed, transformed, and then expanded again, while preserving the semantic integrity of the data. This method works very well when analyzing
univariate time series
, where the relationship between the elements of the sequence is homogeneous. However, the market is more complex than that. We are dealing with a multimodal temporal structure in which interconnected processes — price, volume, volatility, liquidity, open interest, and many other features — unfold in parallel.
Attempting to analyze each of these channels independently, as a separate univariate sequence, results in the loss of critical information. There is a close, dynamic relationship among these features: changes in volume affect the amplitude of price fluctuations, volatility determines the market’s rhythm, and liquidity determines the depth of the market’s reaction to external influences. When these signals are processed separately, this interrelationship breaks down, and the model loses its ability to perceive
the structural integrity of market behavior
.
To address this shortcoming, in our implementation we introduce
a second Bottleneck
that operates on a transposed representation of the original tensor. Unlike standard analysis of univariate sequences, this block examines the data on a per-time-step basis, analyzing all channels simultaneously at each point in time. This allows the model to identify cross-channel relationships, track their dynamics, and account for the complex interactions between features.
At the same time, we retain only one
Residual
block to avoid unduly amplifying the influence of residual connections. This approach strikes a balance between preserving information about past states and efficiently processing new signal combinations. As a result, the model can simultaneously:
extract local patterns within each univariate sequence;
capture inter-channel dependencies and the coordinated dynamics of features;
maintain robustness to noise and an excess of signals by limiting residual connections.
The hybrid approach transforms the
SEW ResNeXt
architecture into a tool capable of
seeing the market
as a complex dynamic system: each feature is interconnected with the others, and changes to a single element are reflected throughout the entire model structure.
The next important aspect to discuss is the choice of an
element-wise spike-combination function
for our three information streams. From the perspective of a risk-oriented approach and the binary nature of spikes,
element-wise multiplication
appears to be an attractive option. In this case, the signal is passed through only when it is confirmed across all streams simultaneously. This principle can be compared to a cautious trader who opens a position only when every indicator has confirmed the signal.
At first glance, the solution seems logical and rigorous — the model responds only to consistent information, thereby reducing the risk of false positives. However, it is worth taking a closer look at how
the error gradient
is distributed in this case.
If the signal is confirmed across all information streams, the error gradient is distributed evenly. However, if at least one stream has not generated a spike, the gradient is directed exclusively toward that stream, while the others receive zero correction. From a logical standpoint, this makes sense. When at least one stream returns zero, there is no downstream signal, and that particular stream requires correction. The error gradient signals that the given stream
needs to be activated
.
The problem arises in the critical case, when
all information streams remain closed
. In this scenario, each element of the element-wise multiplication is zero, and the error gradient, multiplied by these zeros, is completely blocked. As a result, the neuron stops receiving feedback — it is
dead
, and its parameters degrade. In practice, this can cause
training to stop
for part of the network or even the entire model, especially if such situations occur frequently.
In other words, strict element-wise multiplication becomes a trap for training. It protects against false signals, but at the same time creates
the risk of neurons shutting down completely
.
The unimpeded propagation of error gradients is ensured by
simple summation of values
, as implemented in the classic
ResNet
. This approach ensures that even if all information streams are temporarily blocked, the error gradient will be able to adjust the neuron's parameters, and training will continue without interruption.
However, this conflicts with the concept of spikes. Unlike a binary signal of “0” or “1,” the sum of several active streams can result in values of 2 or 3. This disrupts the spiking nature of the activation and can lead to undesirable
oversignaling
, where the model responds too sharply. In market terms, this is similar to a trader who opens a position with excessive confidence without any real data to back it up.
After weighing all the risks, we arrived at a more balanced design: we normalize the sum of the values of the information streams and then apply
spiking activation
. This allows us to simultaneously preserve the binary interpretation of the signal and ensure the correct propagation of error gradients. Normalization limits the resulting value to an acceptable range, preventing excessive responses, and also makes it possible to generate
a reverse signal
. This signal arises when multiple streams simultaneously block activation, and the network receives information indicating that
reverse correction
is necessary. Analogous to a cautious trader who reduces their position when faced with sharp opposition from market signals.
Top-Level Module
To implement the proposed concept in practice, we created a new object,
CNeuronSpikeResNeXtBlock
, which neatly integrates all the key elements of our architecture.

It is based on two
Bottleneck
blocks, one
Residual
block, and transposed representations of the input data, which allows it to account for individual univariate sequences and complex cross-channel interactions. By extending
CNeuronSpikeActivation
, this class preserves the spiking nature of the signals and integrates gates with adaptive thresholds, enabling neurons to respond flexibly to changes in market dynamics.
One of the block's key elements is a dynamic array for storing pointers to
cG
spike-combination function objects, which significantly expands the block's capabilities and opens up room for experimentation. This array makes it possible to connect and use various methods of element-wise signal combination, including both simple summation and normalized combination followed by
spiking activation
. Thanks to this design, the block becomes not just a fixed structure, but a flexible platform for testing various signal integration strategies, adapting to the specific characteristics of particular market data.
The preparation of a new block is entirely handled by the
Init
method, which is responsible for initializing all of its key components and configuring how they interact.

return
false
;
Its algorithm begins by calling the method of the same name in the parent class, providing the foundation for
spiking processing
and the integration of gates with adaptive thresholds.
Next, the method initializes the transposed representations of the original tensor. The first object prepares the data for univariate sequence analysis, while the second performs the inverse transposition of the data. This approach allows the model to simultaneously account for the structure of individual information streams and the interactions between them, laying the foundation for the correct propagation of signals and gradients.
uint
index =
0
;

0

0

false
;

, index, OpenCL, chanels_out, units_out, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
The next step is to initialize the
Bottleneck
blocks. The first Bottleneck processes classic univariate sequences, identifying local patterns in the signals, while the second works with a transposed representation, capturing inter-channel dependencies and the coordinated dynamics of features. Each block receives the channel parameters, the number of groups, and the group size, as well as the necessary optimization parameters and batch size.
index++;
if
(!caBottleneck[
0
].Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, chanels_in, chanels_out, units_in, units_out,
                            group_size, groups, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   index++;
if
(!caBottleneck[
1
].Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, units_in, units_out, chanels_in, chanels_out,
                            group_size, groups, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
The method then initializes the
Residual
block, which preserves critical residual connections, ensuring stability and a balance between a neuron's memory and adaptability.
index++;
if
(!cResidual.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, chanels_in, chanels_out, units_in, units_out,
                      optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
Finally, the method creates
cG
, which contains a dynamic array of spike-combination function objects. Here, a base neuron without activation and a batch normalization object are added sequentially. This sequence allows signals from different information streams to be correctly summed and normalized.
CNeuronBaseOCL*      neuron =
NULL
;
   CNeuronBatchNormOCL* norm =
NULL
;
   cG.Clear();

   neuron =
new
CNeuronBaseOCL();
if
(!neuron ||

0
, index, OpenCL, Neurons(), optimization, iBatch) ||

return
false
;
     }

//---
if
(!cResidual.SetGradient(neuron.getGradient(),
true
) ||
      !caTranspose[
1

true
) ||

0

true

return
false
;
//---
index++;

new
CNeuronBatchNormOCL();

0

return
false

In addition, the block provides synchronization of pointers to error gradient buffers for key components, which ensures correct error propagation throughout the network without unnecessary data copying and prevents signal degradation.
As a result, the
Init
method creates a fully ready block in which every component is initialized, configured, and connected to the others.
The forward pass of the signals is implemented in the
feedForward
method, which ensures sequential processing of information through all key components of the
SEW ResNeXt
block.
bool
CNeuronSpikeResNeXtBlock::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!caTranspose[
0
].FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
First, the data passes through the first transposed block, creating a representation of time steps for further analysis. The signal is then processed sequentially by the first
Bottleneck
module, which identifies local patterns in univariate sequences.
if
(!caBottleneck[
0
].FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
The second
Bottleneck
, in turn, operates on the output of the transposed block, capturing inter-channel dependencies and the coordinated dynamics of features.
if
(!caBottleneck[
1
].FeedForward(caTranspose[
0
].AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!caTranspose[
1
].FeedForward(caBottleneck[
1
].AsObject()))
return
false
;
The information then passes through a second transposed block, preparing it for integration with the residual connections provided by the
Residual
block*.
if
(!cResidual.FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
The next step involves combining the spikes. Signals from both the
Bottleneck
and
Residual
blocks are summed.
CNeuronBaseOCL* current = cG[
0
];
if
(!current)
return
false
;
if
(!SumAndNormilize(caBottleneck[
0
].getOutput(), caTranspose[
1
].getOutput(),
                       current.getOutput(), caTranspose[
1
].GetCount(),
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
) ||
      !SumAndNormilize(current.getOutput(), cResidual.getOutput(),
                       current.getOutput(), caTranspose[
1
].GetCount(),
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
This approach allows both univariate and inter-channel signals to be correctly integrated, preserving the binary nature of spikes and preventing neuron degradation.
Next, the remaining elements of the
cG
array undergo their own forward pass, where each object receives the output of the previous neuron as its input, ensuring the sequential propagation of signals through all combination functions.
for
(
int
i =
1
; i < cG.Total(); i++)
     {
      current = cG[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.FeedForward(cG[i -
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
//---
return
CNeuronSpikeActivation::feedforward(cG[-
1
]);
  }
The process concludes by calling the method of the same name in the parent class, which performs the final processing of the spiking signals and passes the results to the next level of the model.
Thus, the forward pass algorithm ensures smooth, structured signal propagation through all components of the block, integrating local and inter-channel dependencies, normalizing the combined spikes, and preserving correct propagation of error gradients for training. In a market context, this allows the model to respond simultaneously to local changes in each data stream and to the coordinated dynamics of the features, creating a stable and adaptive system for analyzing financial data.
Correct gradient distribution is implemented in the
calcInputGradients
method, which ensures consistent and coordinated updating of the parameters of all components in the
SEW ResNeXt
block.
bool
CNeuronSpikeResNeXtBlock::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!NeuronOCL)
return
false
;
The method begins by verifying the validity of the pointer to the source data object and calling the method of the same name in the parent class, which ensures that gradients are propagated correctly up to the last layer of the
cG
spike combination module.
if
(!CNeuronSpikeActivation::calcInputGradients(cG[-
1
]))
return
false
;
Next, we iterate through all elements of the dynamic
cG
array in reverse order, from last to first, computing the hidden gradients of each neuron based on the output of the next neuron in the chain.
CNeuronBaseOCL* current =
NULL
;
for
(
int
i = cG.Total() -
2
; i >=
0
; i--)
     {
      current = cG[i];
if
(!current ||
         !current.CalcHiddenGradients(cG[i +
1
]))
return
false
;
     }
This approach allows the error to be correctly distributed across all combination and normalization functions, ensuring consistent learning at the spike level.
It should be noted here that, because the pointers to the error-gradient buffers of the main components are swapped, once the error is propagated to the first element of the
cG
array, it is automatically propagated to all information streams within the block. This technique ensures that each stream receives the correct feedback without the need to manually synchronize the gradients for each component. As a result, error propagation occurs naturally and continuously, ensuring consistent training across the entire block structure and preventing neuron degradation even in the presence of complex, interdependent signals.
The resulting gradients are then passed to the second
Bottleneck
and the transposed block, capturing the effect of inter-channel dependencies on the model's error.
if
(!caBottleneck[
1
].CalcHiddenGradients(caTranspose[
1
].AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!caTranspose[
0
].CalcHiddenGradients(caBottleneck[
1
].AsObject()))
return
false
;
The backpropagated error is then propagated through the
Residual
block, which allows the residual connections to be adjusted without unduly amplifying the influence of previous signals.
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(cResidual.AsObject()))
return
false
;
Special attention has been paid to ensuring the accurate storage of data from all information streams. To do this, a temporary data buffer is used, which collects information about the error and correctly feeds it back to the inputs. This prevents the formation of
dead neurons
, ensuring stable and continuous learning even when signals are temporarily absent in individual streams.
CBufferFloat* temp = NeuronOCL.getGradient();
if
(!NeuronOCL.SetGradient(caTranspose[
0
].getPrevOutput(),
false
))
return
false
;
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(caBottleneck[
0
].AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!SumAndNormilize(temp, NeuronOCL.getGradient(), temp,
                       caTranspose[
0
].GetWindow(),
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(caTranspose[
0
].AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!SumAndNormilize(temp, NeuronOCL.getGradient(), temp,
                       caTranspose[
0
].GetWindow(),
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
if
(!NeuronOCL.SetGradient(temp,
false
))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
As a result, the
calcInputGradients
method ensures consistent and safe distribution of error gradients across all components of the block, from transposed sequences and
Bottleneck
modules to
Residual
and the spike combination block. This mechanism ensures that each neuron receives sufficient feedback, adjusts its parameters, and maintains the adaptability of the model, which is capable of analyzing complex multimodal market sequences.

CNeuronSpikeResNeXtBlock

Model Architecture
The next step in our work is to design the architecture of the trainable models. As before, we continue to work within the
Actor-Critic
framework, developing a model capable of making trading decisions independently and responding to market changes. We integrate all previously implemented
SEW ResNeXt
approaches into the
Environment State Encoder
, which acts as the model’s
sensory organ
, accumulating and processing all incoming market information.

The
Actor
and
Critic
architectures have been ported entirely from previous works without any changes, preserving their time-tested structure and functionality. You can find them in the attachment to this article. Thanks to this organization, our model receives a powerful
Encoder
capable of capturing complex temporal and cross-channel market dependencies, while the
Actor
and
Critic
use this representation for accurate forecasting and trading decisions.
Testing
We have completed a major effort to integrate the key components of the
SEW ResNeXt
framework, and now it is time to evaluate the effectiveness of the solutions we have implemented. Before entrusting the model with real funds, it is necessary to thoroughly test the strategy using historical and simulated data, as if honing the skills of an experienced trader and verifying its ability to perform under a wide variety of market conditions. Each stage simulates a live market, allowing the model to gradually gain experience, learn to distinguish signals from noise, and develop robust behavioral algorithms necessary for operating in a real trading environment.
The first stage —
offline training
— is based on historical data for the
EURUSD
currency pair on the
H1
timeframe for the period from
January 2024
through
June 2025
. This period served as a real training ground. The model was trained to reproduce historical patterns, understand price dynamics and trading volumes, and identify regularities and dependencies among key features. It could be said that the model developed a trader's intuition combined with precise strategic judgment. It gradually developed the ability to anticipate market movements and assess the risk of each potential trade.
The next stage —
online fine-tuning
in the
MetaTrader
5 Strategy Tester — will allow the model to work with real-time data streams, candle by candle. Here, it masters the dynamics of the real market, learns to remain stable amid market noise, adjust its actions under low liquidity, and react instantly to sharp price spikes. This stage served as a sort of final refinement of the strategy. The basic structure, built on historical data, remained unchanged, but the model learned to respond flexibly to current market conditions, minimizing the risk of overfitting and improving the accuracy of forecasts even in a volatile environment.
The final test was conducted using data from
July–September 2025
— data that was entirely new and had not been used before. All parameters obtained in the previous stages were loaded without modification, which ensured a fair assessment of the model's ability to generalize. Test results confirm that a step-by-step approach to training and adaptation enables the model to analyze the market and generate a forecast of the upcoming movement of key market features, which can be relied upon when making real trading decisions.
The balance and equity chart shows steady capital growth throughout virtually the entire testing period. Despite occasional drawdowns, equity remains close to the balance. This indicates a prudent and controlled risk management strategy. The maximum equity drawdown was 47.73%, which is quite high under volatile conditions but is consistent with the test scenarios for a time period characterized by sharp price fluctuations.
Total profit amounted to
21.61 USD
on an initial deposit of
100.0 USD
, representing capital growth of more than 20% over the period under review. The
Profit Factor
is
1.15.
This indicates that total profits exceed total losses, and the
Sharpe
ratio of
9.61
demonstrates the strategy’s high risk-adjusted performance. The
Recovery Factor
is
0.42.
It reflects the need to focus on drawdown management when extrapolating to larger amounts of capital.
The model executed 130 trades, of which slightly more than half were profitable (
53.08%
), and the average profit per trade was
2.34 USD
, while the average loss was
2.29 USD
. The longest winning streak was 7 trades, with a total profit of
11.86 USD
, while the longest losing streak was 9 trades, with a total loss of
21.36 USD
. These metrics demonstrate the strategy's moderate aggressiveness and the model's ability to adapt to short-term market fluctuations.
It is worth paying special attention to the even distribution of trades between short and long positions:
69 short trades and 61 long trades
, with success rates of
53.62%
and
52.46%
, respectively. This indicates that the model behaves in a balanced manner across various market scenarios and is capable of responding to both rising and falling prices.
Overall, the test results confirm the viability of the constructed framework based on
SEW ResNeXt
with elements of spiking activation. The model demonstrates stability, adaptability to market dynamics, and sound risk management, making it suitable for further work under real-world financial market conditions.
Conclusion
We have completed the practical implementation of the approaches proposed by the authors of the
SEW Res

for: The model demonstrates robustness to noise and the ability to identify subtle patterns — the very faint signals that herald the emergence of a trend.

The adaptive threshold changes depending on the intensity of the input pulses and the frequency of the spikes. As a result, the network learns to respond only when it is truly necessary, avoiding overfitting to random price fluctuations.

The gating mechanism determines how strongly the current signal should affect the buildup of membrane potential... giving the system dynamic flexibility. It is capable of responding differently to recurring and new patterns, gradually developing its own sense of habituation to similar events.

The second Bottleneck that operates on a transposed representation of the original tensor... examines the data on a per-time-step basis, analyzing all channels simultaneously at each point in time. This allows the model to identify cross-channel relationships, track their dynamics, and account for the complex interactions between features.

Normalization limits the resulting value to an acceptable range, preventing excessive responses, and also makes it possible to generate a reverse signal. This signal arises when multiple streams simultaneously block activation, and the network receives information indicating that reverse correction is necessary.

Total profit amounted to 21.61 USD on an initial deposit of 100.0 USD, representing capital growth of more than 20% over the period under review. The Profit Factor is 1.15. This indicates that total profits exceed total losses, and the Sharpe ratio of 9.61 demonstrates the strategy’s high risk-adjusted performance.
The model executed 130 trades, of which slightly more than half were profitable (53.08%), and the average profit per trade was 2.34 USD, while the average loss was 2.29 USD.

against: Статья не содержит конкретного торгового сигнала: нет чёткого правила входа (например, 'открыть лонг при условии X, Y, Z'), только описание архитектуры нейросетевой модели и её компонентов.

Нет описания, как выходные данные модели преобразуются в торговые решения: не указано, какое значение прогноза или скрытого состояния приводит к открытию/закрытию позиции, стоп-лоссу или тейк-профиту.
В статье отсутствует формула или логическое условие, определяющее момент входа — вместо этого даётся общее описание обучения, архитектуры и интерпретации через аналогии ('как у опытного трейдера').

Используются данные, недоступные на спот-форексе без биржевого стакана: в тексте прямо указано, что модель обрабатывает 'price, volume, volatility, liquidity, open interest, and many other features', причём подчёркивается необходимость совместного анализа их 'interconnected processes' и 'cross-channel relationships'. Объёмы (volume) и открытый интерес (open interest) в спот-форексе отсутствуют; волатильность и ликвидность — производные величины, требующие либо расчёта по ценовым данным (что допустимо), либо внешних источников (что не указано); но open interest — фьючерсная метрика, недоступная в спот-режиме.
non_fatal: Отсутствует тест вне выборки с указанием OOS-периода — но в статье есть упоминание теста на июль–сентябрь 2025, что формально является OOS; однако неясно, использовались ли эти данные *исключительно* для финальной оценки или частично в fine-tuning.
Не учтены спред и комиссии — но это разрешено не считать фатальным.
Нет деталей реализации стоп-лосса и тейк-профита — но они могут отсутствовать в правиле, это не фатально.

Модель обучается в рамках Actor-Critic RL — это инфраструктура принятия решений, но статья не объясняет, как именно Actor генерирует действия (например, 'long/short/close'), значит, торговое правило не выделено явно — это уже учтено в пункте о невозможности записи входа формулой.
